mcqs.question: Which of these is a service the runtime provides, rather than something the compiler fully resolves ahead of time?
options: Checking that an array index is in bounds before the access executes
Parsing the source file's syntax
Resolving which overloaded method signature matches at a call site
Reporting a syntax error for a missing semicolon
mcqs.explanation: Bounds checking has to happen against the actual array length at the moment of access, which the compiler usually can't prove safe ahead of time, so the runtime enforces it on every access. Parsing, overload resolution, and syntax errors are all compile-time work.

mcqs.question: A program throws a NullPointerException in production. What does that tell you about the compile-time/run-time split?
options: The compiler failed to catch a bug it should have caught
The JIT deoptimized a speculative assumption
The runtime's safety check fired because the compiler couldn't statically prove the reference was non-null
The garbage collector reclaimed the object too early
mcqs.explanation: Null checks are a runtime responsibility precisely because static analysis generally can't rule out every null path — the compiler lets the code through and the runtime enforces safety at the point of use. This isn't a compiler defect, a GC bug, or deoptimization.

mcqs.question: A team is choosing between a JVM-based service and a Go binary for a latency-sensitive serverless function with frequent cold starts. What's the most accurate framing of the trade-off?
options: Go is a faster language than Java in every case
The JVM provides more safety guarantees, so it is always the better engineering choice
Java's syntax is the bottleneck, not the runtime
Go's native binary skips a persistent runtime layer, which usually wins on cold-start latency at the cost of the managed services (GC, JIT, reflection) the JVM provides
mcqs.explanation: The relevant difference is architectural: a JVM service pays runtime initialization (classloading, heap setup, interpreter warm-up) on every cold start, while a Go binary starts executing native code immediately. That's a genuine trade-off, not a blanket "language X is faster" claim, and it isn't about syntax.

mcqs.question: A microbenchmark measures a Java method's first 50ms of execution and reports it as 20x slower than the equivalent C function. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Java's bytecode format is inherently 20x less efficient than native code
The measurement is dominated by runtime warm-up — interpreted execution and class loading before the JIT has compiled the hot path
The JVM has a hard-coded 50ms startup penalty per method call
The garbage collector paused for the entire 50ms window
mcqs.explanation: At 50ms, the JIT typically hasn't identified or compiled the method yet, so you're measuring the interpreter plus classloading, not steady-state throughput. There's no per-method fixed penalty, and a full-window GC pause is a much less common explanation than ordinary warm-up.

mcqs.question: Which sequence correctly orders what happens when you run `java Main`?
options: JVM initializes -> bootstrap classloader loads core classes -> your class loads and links -> main runs interpreted
main runs immediately -> classes load lazily only if main throws
The OS interprets the bytecode directly, bypassing the JVM
Your class loads first, then the JVM initializes its heap to match
mcqs.explanation: The JVM has to exist and initialize its own core services before it can load and verify even its own bootstrap classes, and your class loads and links after that, before main executes any bytecode. The OS never interprets bytecode itself, and the JVM's heap setup precedes any class loading, not the reverse.
